attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, stated as his own view.

semantics.note: Keeps the link that the misreading served the defamation. Firm past-tense observation.

contract.note: Reading 'defamed' in its everyday sense rather than as a court finding is the ordinary reading. Letting one connected incident satisfy the generic plural is reasonable and fair to him.

evidence.note: Contemporaneous firsthand report, April 5, 2023, that Bing claimed Turley was accused of harassment and cited Turley's own op-ed as its source.
The cited op-ed itself, which explicitly denies the accusation. This confirms that Bing reversed its meaning. It is the comparison text, not proof of Bing's output.

reviews.rationale: Within the window, a reporter documented Bing making a false harassment accusation against Turley and citing Turley's own op-ed, which rejects that accusation. That meets the support condition: a false, damaging statement backed by an article saying the opposite. There is no court finding, but the contract does not require one.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. He bases the access premise on rumor but draws the 'Nadella has that right' conclusion himself.

semantics.note: Keeps the rumor qualifier on access. The conclusion that Nadella has the right is stated firmly.

contract.note: Testing whether OpenAI held a contractual approval or safety veto under the 2023 agreement is a fair reading of 'has that right'. The rumor hedge applies to the access premise.

evidence.note: CMA account of the 2023 agreement: exclusive license and independent commercialization, but with an AGI carve-out and restrictions that are redacted. It neither establishes nor rules out a safety veto.
Microsoft's own statement, dated four days after the window, describing independent deployment rights up to AGI. Says nothing on resolving safety disputes.
OpenAI's announcement of the renewed partnership. Says nothing about deployment authority in a disagreement.

reviews.rationale: The evidence shows broad licensing and independent commercialization. But the restrictions are redacted, and nothing shows whether OpenAI could block a Microsoft deployment on safety grounds. The packet cannot settle either the support or the contradiction condition.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: Keeps his 'I don't see any reason' framing. The checkable part is his unhedged comparison with Apple App Store apps.

contract.note: Reading the claim as substantially weaker isolation and review than Apple's system, judged across the plugin system, is an ordinary reading and fair to him.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own account of sandboxing for its hosted code interpreter. Says nothing about third-party plugin controls or how they compare with Apple.
Apple's own account of App Store review. Covers only the Apple side of the comparison.
Apple's May 2022 security guide on app sandboxing, from before the window. Covers only Apple's side.
Research documenting a June 7, 2023 plugin privacy failure. No matched comparison with Apple.

reviews.rationale: The packet documents Apple's controls and some plugin weaknesses, but has no contemporary account of OpenAI's plugin review and enforcement and no common security measure for the two. The system-wide comparison cannot be settled on this evidence.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: Describes the capabilities plugins had at the time and the risks they created. 'Any security professional' is rhetorical emphasis.

contract.note: Reading the capabilities as existing across the plugin ecosystem, and phishing as an example rather than a named incident, is an ordinary reading of his words.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own launch documentation shows browsing and file upload and download within the window. It also records sandbox limits.
May 2023 demonstration: prompt injection misused a user's delegated Zapier access to read email and exfiltrate it. Zapier later added a mitigation.
September 2023 research describing phishing and account-hijack mechanisms. Not tied to a specific event before June 8.

reviews.rationale: Documentation shows internet access and file handling in the plugin release period, and a dated demonstration shows plugins misusing delegated user authority to expose private data. That meets the support condition. No phishing incident is shown, but the contract treats phishing as an example. Sandbox limits narrow the claim's scope but do not contradict it.
